rationale: A wins because it finds the harder story hiding in plain sight: “the pairing” of a 100-store robot rollout and a price freeze, then forces the margin question without pretending the answer is known. B is useful, but “Chipotle says it won't raise prices this year, even as its food costs climb” separates the price story from the automation story and loses the sharpest editorial tension. A also does better reporter-proof hygiene: its “What is the baseline behind ‘roughly halves’?” question is exactly the kind of thing that stops a founder from walking into a buzzsaw.
gaps_in_A: “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” overreaches. The update says Chipotle is testing Digital Makeline, not that it is proving a full assembly-line architecture.

“Both the 100-restaurant rollout and the price-freeze commitment are live company news as of today” is inferred from current time and the update, but “today” is not explicitly stated in the fact block.

“If food-cost inflation, restaurant labor, or automation is live in the news this week” is a valid caveat, but the next step leans on newsjacking when the supplied update is self-contained company news.
gaps_in_B: “food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory” is outside the supplied facts. It may be true, but this judge can’t credit unsourced category lore.
“inflation coverage gives it immediate context” smuggles in a live media peg that was not supplied. The update says food-cost inflation exists; it does not say coverage is live this week.

“Autocado halves guac prep time” as a standalone data angle — `duplicate` is too quick. The baseline, methodology, and service-speed conversion could support a distinct ops/data angle, and A correctly keeps it.
“Next step: `journalist-fit-check`” is premature. B has unresolved proof holes and no live-news check; resolving names before tightening the angle risks operationalizing a soft story.
